newsitem.title: UK: Copper slips on slow LME, tightness eases.
newsitem.headline: Copper slips on slow LME, tightness eases.

text.p: Base metal prices veered lower during routine Friday LME ring trading, with a mini-reaction setting in after Thursday's gains, while copper tightness drew to a close,

Copper was seeing some profit-taking after the previous session's run-up to near $2,300, with a 3,250-tonne net increase in warehouse stocks much as expected. There were few surprises in the data, although some traders noted that there were 4,625 tonnes taken out of inventory.
"It came out of a good spread of locations, which could be a sign that consumers are picking stuff up now that the tightness is passing," one said.

However, for the market to sustain advances towards $2,300 there will need to be some further interest from the Chinese. Recent activity, on both sides of the market, has not been significant, and it may need the end of China's New Year holidays to bring about the major buying that has been talked about, they said.
Meanwhile, the period of severe technical tightness that has enveloped the market since Jan 29 is reaching an end. Cash/one day traded at $22.50 backwardation, against the LME's limit of $24.

But next week, daily premiums will be back to single figures. Monday is pricing for the February date - third Wednesday - and the rate for the whole week is just $1 backwardation. February/March is $16/17. The cash/threes premium was back at $86/96, against $100 on Thursday.
There are periods of congestion around early-March, but tightness then may not be so fierce as the tonnages that were restricted during the last two weeks may be more freely available.
Last three months business this morning was at $2,263 a tonne, a $12 loss from the previous day's kerb.

Elsewhere, profit-taking hit zinc after Thursday's run-up to new two-year highs, but a solid undertone remained in the market, following a 1,225-tonne stock decline. Prices closed the kerb at $1,215, down $6.

Aluminium sagged under commission house sales and disappointed liquidation after the market failed to respond to a 9,975-tonne stock draw. The market was not helped also by news that Norsk Hydro is to re-start idled capacity, albeit only 20,000 tonnes annually. Final kerb trade was at $1,565, down $11.
Nickel skidded lower as well, not helped by a 720-tonne inventory increase, and prices closed the kerb at $7,740, down $140. But consumer buying helped lift tin to $6,010, up $70.
Lead interest was slack, and three months prices closed the session at a steadier $659/60, while alloy was marked down with primary to $1,475/80.
